Translation drift is this track's main failure mode and this line has a rival translation in the field, so that is where I attacked. Rees's Penguin version of 1995 reads What saves you is to take one step. Then another. It's always the same step, but you have to take it. If the proposal were carrying Rees's sense in Galantiere's name, or a hybrid of the two, the line would be dead. It is not.

WHAT I DID. I read the Galantiere text in this session's scratch directory, whose title page gives Wind, Sand and Stars by Antoine de St. Exupery, First Published 1939, Translated from the French by Lewis Galantiere, and whose contents list runs 1. The Craft, 2. The Men, 3. The Tool, 4. The Elements, 5. The Plane and the Planet, 6. Oasis, 7. Men of the Desert, 8. Prisoner of the Sand, 9. Barcelona and Madrid, 10. Conclusion. The sentence sits inside Guillaumet's quoted account of the Andes, in its own paragraph and inside its own quotation marks: “What saves a man is to take a step. Then another step. It is always the same step, but you have to take it.” Exact, to the comma. The next paragraph is “I swear that what I went through, no animal would have gone through,” which the narrator then calls the noblest sentence ever spoken, and a few lines further he addresses the pilot by name, And it was in these words, Guillaumet, that you expressed your pride. The evidence block describes this correctly.

LOCATOR. I checked the chapter boundaries by line number rather than taking the verifier's word: chapter 2 opens where The Men begins and runs to the head of 3. The Tool, and the passage falls comfortably inside it, in the pages that open Guillaumet, old friend, of you too I shall say a few words. So ch. 2, The Men is right, and the verifier's correction away from Prisoner of the Sand, which is chapter 8 and the Libya crash, was the correct correction. Generalising note, since it is the trap that produced the original error: in this book the Andes story is Guillaumet's and belongs to The Men, while the desert story is the author's own and belongs to Prisoner of the Sand.

SPEAKER. It is Guillaumet's direct speech, printed in quotation marks, so naming him in parentheses after the locator is required and is done.

OTHER GATES. shipped.js: shipped empty, near empty, antoine de saint-exupery at 1 of 3 and that one in May, so under the year cap and not twice in this month. Not banned. The misattribution list does name Saint-Exupery, but for a different line, the ship-building paraphrase from Citadelle; this one is not a paraphrase, it is the printed translation. Scope: 1939, not scripture, film, lyric, proverb, business or oratory. Publishable: the chapter describes exhaustion and frostbitten feet, but the quotation carries none of it and needs no warning. Source line is 107 characters, leads with the name, no dash, no straight quote, and runs work, locator, speaker, translation, which is rule 5's order. Theme fit is the best kind for July: it is what a man said about walking out of the Andes, and it tells the reader at six in the morning what to do next.

TWO NOTE-LEVEL FIXES I WOULD MAKE BEFORE IT SHIPS, NEITHER OF THEM A REFUTATION. First, the note says Guillaumet spoke the words at Mendoza. The text does not say that. Mendoza is where the narrator waited and searched from; the speech is reported in retrospect with no place attached, so the note should say he spoke them after walking out of the Andes and stop there. Second, the tag Essay: Wind, Sand and Stars is memoir and reportage rather than essay, but the vocabulary is closed and Essay is the only prose tag that can hold it, so keep it and let the fiction-essay lane count it.
